study.title: The Instant and Sustained Effect of Electroacupuncture in Postgraduate Students with Depression: An fMRI Study
study.randomization: not randomized; study described as quasi-experimental
study.population: Chinese postgraduate students with mild depression
study.inclusion_criteria: 1) all subjects were all at least 18 years old, right-handed, and were educated to postgraduate level; 2) all subjects had 7–24 points according to the HRSD-17; and 3) had not taken any analgesics, psychotropic drugs, anti-inflammatory drugs or vasoactive drugs, and had not received any acupuncture treatment during the past 2 weeks before enrollment
study.exclusion_criteria: 1) cannot stand acupuncture stimulation; 2) excessive head motion during MR scan; and 3) brain structure abnormality

arms.arm_label_exact: postgraduate students with mild depression receiving electroacupuncture at GV20
arms.dropouts: 2 subjects excluded due to brain structure abnormality

interventions.penetration_exact: penetrating; tip bent 15° to the front to reach the aponeurosis cap
interventions.manipulation_exact: needle handle connected to low-frequency pulse therapy instrument (Huatuo brand, Model G6805-2, Suzhou China) through a special wire; continuous wave, frequency 2Hz, current 3mA, take the endurance of the subjects as the limit
interventions.deqi_intended_exact: acupuncture sensation of soreness assessed by VAS after experiment
interventions.electrical_intensity_exact: 3mA, take the endurance of the subjects as the limit
interventions.session_duration_exact: EA stimulation duration 5 minutes; whole procedure lasted 40 min
interventions.practitioner_description_exact: an experienced (more than 5 years) and licensed acupuncturist
interventions.participant_instructions_exact: keep their eyes closed and stay awake during the scanning process; be relaxed and breathe peacefully with their heads fixed by foam headrests to reduce active or passive movements
interventions.treatment_rationale_given_exact: GV20 widely used to treat mental disorders in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM); single acupoint selected to clarify specificity of this acupoint

extraction_notes.note: No sham or control arm was included; this is a single-arm within-subject quasi-experimental study. Therefore, comparisons are entirely within-subject across phases (baseline, during EA, post-EA). The lack of a sham control is a notable limitation for inferring causality.
Expectancy, credibility, and blinding assessments were not reported. No instrument was used or referenced for these constructs.

Table 2 lists mean ReHo values (Z-transformed) for Phase I, II, III across all significant clusters identified in the ANOVA. The pairwise comparisons in Table 3 report mean difference ReHo values with p-values, but do not list separate coordinates per pairwise comparison beyond those already in Table 2. It is assumed coordinates are shared from ANOVA clusters.

The paper reports 'Phase III < phase II' for PCUN.R/PCC.R and ANG.R with mean differences and p<0.001 (Table 3), but no corresponding entry for 'Phase II > Phase I' for PCUN.R/PCC.R or ANG.R appears in Table 3. This suggests these regions did not show significant change from Phase I to Phase II (text confirms: 'while no significantly decreased brain was found'). Extraction reflects this.
extraction_notes.source_location: Results/ReHo Results and Table 3, pages 4 and 8

extraction_notes.note: The paper does not report a correlation between Phase II (instant effect) ReHo values and VAS or HRSD-17 scores. Correlation results in Figure 7 are limited to Phase I (for ANG.R vs HRSD) and Phase III (multiple regions vs VAS and HRSD).
extraction_notes.source_location: Figure 7 and Results/Correlation section, pages 5 and 8

extraction_notes.note: The cluster extent threshold used was 'cluster > 39' (voxels) in the ANOVA, but the pairwise comparisons used Bonferroni correction (p < 0.05; p < 0.0033 after correction). It is not entirely clear if the same spatial extent criterion was applied to the pairwise comparisons, as Table 3 does not report cluster sizes for pairwise results.
extraction_notes.source_location: Methods/Statistical Analysis and Table 3, pages 4 and 8

extraction_notes.note: The ANOVA p < 0.001 and the p-value tables note 'Statistical significance level: p<0.0033 (a p < 0.05 with Bonferroni correction was adopted to correct for the number of tests)'. The exact number of tests being corrected for (presumably 15 pairwise combinations or 5 regions × 3 pairwise comparisons) is not specified in the text.

The paper states diagnosis was confirmed using 'structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID)' but no further clinical characterization data (e.g., comorbidities, duration of illness, prior treatments) are reported beyond HRSD-17 scores.
No information about randomization or allocation sequence is provided. The study explicitly uses a 'quasi-experimental' design without a control group. There is no mention of random assignment.

Figure 3 (ANOVA result brain map), Figure 4 (Phase II > Phase I), Figure 5 (Phase III < Phase II), Figure 6 (Phase III vs Phase I), and Figure 7 (correlation plots) are described but coordinates for displayed clusters are only available in Tables 2 and 3, not from the figures themselves.

The VAS in this paper measures 'acupuncture sensation of soreness' scored by the acupuncturist after the experiment. It is not a standard patient-reported pain scale. Caution is needed when comparing to self-reported VAS measures in other studies.
The paper does not provide individual subject demographic or clinical data. Group means are available only in Table 1.
PMID is not reported in the accessible document text. The DOI is stated in the header/footer as http://doi.org/10.2147/NDT.S307083.
